summary.text: Exact divisibility is obtained by comparing every prime valuation: at each prime-power level the numerator contributes \(\lfloor N/q^i\rfloor^2\), while the denominator contributes \(\sum_{m\le M}m\lfloor M/m\rfloor\le M^2\), with \(M=\lfloor N/q^i\rfloor\). For \(N=np+k\) with \(k<p\), none of the newly added integers is divisible by \(p\), so the numerator valuation is unchanged, and Legendre’s factorial-valuation formula makes the denominator valuation depend only on the quotients \(\lfloor N/p^i\rfloor=\lfloor np/p^i\rfloor\); subtracting these valuations proves the claim.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
A_N:=\prod_{j=1}^N\prod_{r=1}^N \gcd(j,r),
\qquad
D_N:=\prod_{m=1}^N\left(\left\lfloor\frac Nm\right\rfloor!\right)^m.
\]
Thus the sequence in the statement is
\[
a(N)=\frac{A_N}{D_N}.
\]
We will first prove that this quotient is an integer, and then compare its \(p\)-adic valuation at \(N=np\) and \(N=np+k\).

For a prime \(q\) and a positive integer \(x\), write \(v_q(x)\) for the exponent of \(q\) in the prime factorization of \(x\). We shall use two valuation formulas. All sums below can be viewed as sums over all \(i\geq 1\), because their terms are zero once \(q^i>N\); equivalently, one may truncate every sum at any sufficiently large bound, for example at \(i=N\) when \(N>0\).

**1. The valuation of the numerator.**

We claim that for every prime \(q\),
\[
 v_q(A_N)=\sum_{i\geq 1}\left\lfloor\frac{N}{q^i}\right\rfloor^2. \tag{1}
\]
Indeed, for positive \(j,r\),
\[
v_q(\gcd(j,r))=\min(v_q(j),v_q(r)).
\]
For any nonnegative integers \(u,v\),
\[
\min(u,v)=\sum_{i\geq 1}{\bf 1}_{i\leq u}{\bf 1}_{i\leq v}.
\]
Consequently,
\[
v_q(\gcd(j,r))
 =\sum_{i\geq 1}{\bf 1}_{q^i\mid j}{\bf 1}_{q^i\mid r}.
\]
Summing this over all ordered pairs \((j,r)\) with \(1\leq j,r\leq N\), and interchanging finite sums, gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
v_q(A_N)
&=\sum_{i\geq 1}
 \left(\sum_{j=1}^N {\bf 1}_{q^i\mid j}\right)
 \left(\sum_{r=1}^N {\bf 1}_{q^i\mid r}\right).
\end{aligned}
\]
There are exactly \(\lfloor N/q^i\rfloor\) multiples of \(q^i\) in \(\{1,\dots,N\}\). This proves (1).

**2. The valuation of the denominator.**

We claim that
\[
 v_q(D_N)
 =\sum_{i\geq 1}\sum_{m=1}^{\lfloor N/q^i\rfloor}
 m\left\lfloor\frac{\lfloor N/q^i\rfloor}{m}\right\rfloor. \tag{2}
\]
By Legendre's formula,
\[
v_q(t!)=\sum_{i\geq 1}\left\lfloor\frac{t}{q^i}\right\rfloor.
\]
Therefore, using additivity of valuations on products and the rule
\(v_q(x^m)=m v_q(x)\),
\[
\begin{aligned}
v_q(D_N)
&=\sum_{m=1}^N m\,v_q\!\left(\left\lfloor\frac Nm\right\rfloor!\right)\\
&=\sum_{m=1}^N m\sum_{i\geq 1}
  \left\lfloor\frac{\lfloor N/m\rfloor}{q^i}\right\rfloor. \tag{3}
\end{aligned}
\]
For positive integers \(m,s\), iterated integer division satisfies
\[
\left\lfloor\frac{\lfloor N/m\rfloor}{s}\right\rfloor
 =\left\lfloor\frac{N}{ms}\right\rfloor
 =\left\lfloor\frac{\lfloor N/s\rfloor}{m}\right\rfloor. \tag{4}
\]
For completeness, the first equality follows because, for any integer \(t\),
\[
t\leq \frac{\lfloor N/m\rfloor}{s}
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
mst\leq N,
\]
and the same characterization proves the second equality.

Apply (4) with \(s=q^i\), and interchange the finite sums in (3). If
\[
M_i:=\left\lfloor\frac N{q^i}\right\rfloor,
\]
then the summand is
\[
m\left\lfloor\frac{M_i}{m}\right\rfloor.
\]
It is zero for \(m>M_i\). Thus the inner sum over \(1\leq m\leq N\) can be restricted to \(1\leq m\leq M_i\), proving (2).

**3. The ratio is an integer.**

Fix a prime \(q\). For every nonnegative integer \(M\), define
\[
S(M):=\sum_{m=1}^M m\left\lfloor\frac Mm\right\rfloor.
\]
For each \(m\geq1\),
\[
m\left\lfloor\frac Mm\right\rfloor\leq M.
\]
There are \(M\) terms, so
\[
S(M)\leq M^2. \tag{5}
\]
Combining (1), (2), and (5), with \(M_i=\lfloor N/q^i\rfloor\), yields
\[
\begin{aligned}
v_q(D_N)
&=\sum_{i\geq1}S(M_i)\\
&\leq\sum_{i\geq1}M_i^2\\
&=v_q(A_N).
\end{aligned}
\]
This inequality holds for every prime \(q\). Both \(A_N\) and \(D_N\) are positive integers: every gcd occurring in \(A_N\) is positive, and every factorial occurring in \(D_N\) is positive. By unique prime factorization, a positive integer \(x\) divides a positive integer \(y\) exactly when \(v_q(x)\leq v_q(y)\) for every prime \(q\). Hence
\[
D_N\mid A_N.
\]
Thus \(a(N)=A_N/D_N\) is an integer, and for every prime \(p\),
\[
v_p(a(N))=v_p(A_N)-v_p(D_N). \tag{6}
\]
There is no ambiguity from subtraction here, since the divisibility just proved ensures that the second valuation is at most the first.

**4. Constancy on each block from \(np\) through \(np+p-1\).**

Now let \(n\) be a positive integer, let \(p\) be prime, and let \(k\) satisfy
\[
0\leq k<p.
\]
Set
\[
N_0=np,\qquad N_k=np+k.
\]
The central observation is that for every \(i\geq1\),
\[
\left\lfloor\frac{N_k}{p^i}\right\rfloor
=
\left\lfloor\frac{N_0}{p^i}\right\rfloor. \tag{7}
\]
To see this, first divide by \(p\). Since \(0\leq k<p\), Euclidean division gives
\[
\left\lfloor\frac{np+k}{p}\right\rfloor=n
=\left\lfloor\frac{np}{p}\right\rfloor.
\]
Write \(i=1+r\), where \(r\geq0\). Using the iterated-division identity (4),
\[
\left\lfloor\frac{np+k}{p^{1+r}}\right\rfloor
=
\left\lfloor
\frac{\lfloor(np+k)/p\rfloor}{p^r}
\right\rfloor
=
\left\lfloor\frac n{p^r}\right\rfloor.
\]
The identical calculation for \(np\) has the same result, proving (7).

Apply the numerator formula (1), now with \(q=p\). Equation (7) shows equality term by term, so
\[
v_p(A_{np+k})
 =\sum_{i\geq1}\left\lfloor\frac{np+k}{p^i}\right\rfloor^2
 =\sum_{i\geq1}\left\lfloor\frac{np}{p^i}\right\rfloor^2
 =v_p(A_{np}). \tag{8}
\]

Likewise, formula (2) for the denominator depends on \(N\), for fixed \(p\), only through the values \(\lfloor N/p^i\rfloor\). More explicitly, its \(i\)-th contribution is
\[
S\!\left(\left\lfloor\frac N{p^i}\right\rfloor\right).
\]
By (7), these contributions agree for \(N=np+k\) and \(N=np\), for every \(i\geq1\). Hence
\[
v_p(D_{np+k})=v_p(D_{np}). \tag{9}
\]

Finally, use (6) at the two arguments and then (8) and (9):
\[
\begin{aligned}
v_p(a(np+k))
&=v_p(A_{np+k})-v_p(D_{np+k})\\
&=v_p(A_{np})-v_p(D_{np})\\
&=v_p(a(np)).
\end{aligned}
\]
Because \(k\) was arbitrary with \(0\leq k<p\), this proves
\[
v_p(a(np))=v_p(a(np+1))=\cdots=v_p(a(np+p-1)),
\]
which is precisely conjecture C for A129365.
